title: Intrinsic size specification is not clear with rounding rules
body: ## What is the issue with the HTML Standard? This is a follow-up issue to https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/5574 I've recently looked into properly specifying metadata so browsers show images at natural size. The key specification is here: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/images.html#preparing-an-image-for-presentation However, when testing out various images and browsers, I ran into an issue: Consider the following two cases: 1. For a 800x1200 image at dpi=600, we get 96x144 (XResolution/YResolution) ✅. Everything is nice and rounded, and the image displays correctly in Chrome, Firefox, and Safari. 2. For a 782 × 914 image at dpi=600, we get 93.84x109.44 (XResolution/YResolution). This is not representable in EXIF, as XResolution and YResolution are integers. Image editors will save this as 94x110 (I'm not sure why the latter is rounded up, but that's what image editors produce). The latter image works in Chrome and Firefox, but it does not display at natural size in Safari; Safari seems to reject the EXIF data since it does not fulfill the equality requirement 4.8.4.3.6.13. I think as the spec is currently written, Safari is allowed to reject the EXIF data, but it's not very practical. For mathematical correctness, I believe one approach would be to specify PixelXDensity and PixelYDensity as rationals 56304/94 and 65808/110, but the math still doesn't fully check out because suddenly the DPI is non-uniform, not what the intent was. (and also, images with that EXIF info still don't work in Safari). ## Is this a browser bug? I believe the _intent_ of the spec is clear. However, Safari currently takes it literally, and one could argue its interpretation is correct. So I am reluctant to report a bug to the Safari / Webkit team. ## Ideal outcome I think it would be great if the spec would clarify what "equality" here means; as a floating point and an integer are compared, it's not quite clear. Could mean "really 100% fractional match", could mean "rounded match", could mean "some epsilon is ok". ## Related The tests at http://wpt.live/density-size-correction/density-corrected-size-img.html do not contain an image with resolutions not divisible in the way that the spec currently requires, and so the issue went unnoticed. Here is a comparison, you can see the effect right on GitHub when comparing between browsers: 1. "Roundable" image, as in the test: ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a80175a7-d7ce-4f75-8236-d35e9b45e113) 2. Same image but cropped by one pixel on the left, so there ought to be rounding going on. This is currently displaying at full size (not natural size) in Safari, but as intended (to the best of my understanding) in Chrome and Firefox. ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f118b42e-288b-492b-b106-6b9089ce56da) And here are screenshots from the very test posted above, so you can see the difference immediately – the screenshot from Safari shows that the "roundable" image displays in natural size and the "fractional" image displays in original size, ignoring the EXIF information: | Browser | Screenshot | | - | - | | Chrome | | | Firefox | | | Safari | | ## Literal Interpretation If the specification is to be taken literally, it would require adjusting the DPI of the image to always mathematically match the pixel size. Usually, DPI is specified as a rational like "1440000/10000" or "60000/1000", which matches with the artistic intent of saying "this image is to be used at 144 dpi" or "600 dpi". To get the specification math to work out, one needs to instead specify "mathematically perfect" DPI – a 99x49 image at 144 dpi needs EXIF data as follows: `XResolution = 99 * 72 / 144 = 7128/144` and `YResolution = 49 * 72 / 144 = 3528/144`. This does in fact result in images displaying in natural size in Safari: 144 dpi with `XResolution 7128/144, YResolution 3528/144` ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/952bb781-0bec-4ce9-a439-7396186b8423) 30 dpi with `XResolution 7128/30, YResolution 3528/30` ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a3e0b007-2bd6-42f9-a7ab-4f87c6f5c38c) Unfortunately it also results in images not "roundtripping" in photo editors as expected anymore, since the "exact" DPI may now be different. The 30 DPI image now has 29.95 DPI, which is not what was intended by the author of the file, and not what would be used for e.g. printing the image.
